analysis.one_liner: Blocks new fossil fuel leasing and permitting on federal public lands unless it fits national climate targets.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in either committee or chamber before Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required federal land agencies to manage public lands and waters to cut greenhouse gas emissions in line with the U.S. targets of 50–52% emission reductions by 2030 and net-zero by 2050. It would have stopped new federal lease sales and permits for coal, oil, gas, oil shale, and tar sands until an emissions reduction strategy showed new drilling was consistent with those targets, put every future lease through a "climate test," created a public dashboard of emissions from federal fossil fuel operations, and charged new fees on federal fossil fuel production to help energy-dependent states diversify their economies. It never advanced beyond committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the bill would primarily benefit people exposed to pollution from federal fossil fuel production — which the bill itself notes falls hardest on Tribal nations and environmental justice communities — by cutting lifecycle emissions from coal, oil, and gas extracted from public lands and waters. It would also benefit state and local governments in energy-producing regions through new severance-fee revenues earmarked for economic diversification, and give the public new transparency through a mandatory online dashboard of emissions from every federal fossil fuel operation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near federal fossil fuel extraction

how_it_helps.text: Bars new federal lease sales and permits for coal, oil, natural gas, oil shale, or tar sands until the Interior Department and Forest Service publish an emissions reduction strategy showing that new leasing fits the U.S. targets of 50–52% emissions cuts by 2030, clean electricity by 2035, and net-zero by 2050.

Requires every future federal fossil fuel lease to pass a 'climate test' screening whether its emissions fit those targets and whether the fuel would still be economically viable if the targets are met, with mandatory rejection of proposals that fail.

Requires a public online dashboard of greenhouse gas emissions from every federal fossil fuel operation, including gas vented, flared, or leaked, plus energy produced from federal renewable projects — transparency ordinary people do not currently have.

Imposes annual severance fees on fossil fuels from new federal leases, with the revenue used to help states that depend on federal energy revenues diversify their economies away from coal, oil, and gas.
Requires public meetings, translated materials, and consultation with environmental justice communities, Tribes, labor unions, and state governors in drafting each strategy.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel companies would bear the cost: no new federal leases or permits until a climate-consistency strategy is published, a climate screening test that mandates rejection of noncompliant projects, and annual severance fees on production from new leases. Some energy-dependent state budgets and fossil fuel workers in those states could face reduced federal-lease revenue in the transition, which the bill addresses through diversification funding rather than direct worker support. Consumers could face some near-term energy price pressure.

drawbacks.text: Blocking or conditioning new federal leasing and permitting could raise short-term energy costs for consumers and reduce revenue that some Western states and counties collect from federal oil, gas, and coal production.

The bill concedes that new leasing could resume only if the Interior Secretary finds that lifecycle emissions from new leases are consistent with national climate targets — a determination critics could view as a policy choice embedded in an executive agency rather than a settled fact, and which would be subject to litigation as a final agency action.
The bill does not directly fund retraining or replacement jobs for fossil fuel workers; it directs revenue to state economic diversification, leaving individual workers' transition to others.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — aligning one of the largest sources of U.S. emissions, federal fossil fuel production, with national climate targets, plus transparency and transition funding for energy-dependent states — is substantial and honestly weighed against real costs: possible near-term energy price pressure, lost state and local revenue from federal leasing, and opposition from communities whose payrolls depend on those leases. The bill's transition-fee revenue and economic-resiliency findings partially address those costs, but the burden on fossil-fuel-dependent regions would still be real. The bill also had an escape valve: leasing could resume once officials verified consistency with climate targets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and several subcommittees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended, so it never reached the House floor or the Senate.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 13, 2022, less than four months before the 117th Congress expired.

On introduction it was referred to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees and split among four Natural Resources subcommittees; a month later it was also referred to the Agriculture subcommittee on Conservation and Forestry.
The action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee votes, and no floor action — the last recorded action is the September 29, 2022 subcommittee referral.
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies that lease and drill on federal public lands are better off: no freeze on new leases, no climate screening test, no added severance fees, and no public emissions dashboard was ever adopted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies leasing federal lands

for.name: Rep. Raúl M. Grijalva
for.role: Sponsor; chair of the House Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring federal fossil fuel leasing to align with national climate targets.

for.name: Reps. Alan Lowenthal, Jared Huffman, Katie Porter, Diana DeGette, Mike Levin, and A. Donald McEachin

against.name: House Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; the last recorded action was a subcommittee referral on September 29, 2022.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committee without any recorded votes.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and coal companies operating on federal public lands and waters
industries.note: The bill would block new federal lease sales and permits unless shown to fit national climate targets, subject every new lease to a climate screening test, and add annual severance fees. Federal lands supply a meaningful share of U.S. fossil fuel production, so this directly hits the industry's future supply pipeline.

industries.industry: Renewable energy developers (wind, solar, geothermal on public lands)
industries.note: The bill directs federal agencies to consider public lands' potential for carbon-free energy and to report renewable production publicly, positioning renewables as the preferred use of federal acreage as fossil leasing is curtailed.

industries.industry: State and local governments dependent on federal energy revenues
industries.note: They would lose leasing revenue as new federal leases stop, but new severance fees would fund state economic diversification away from coal, oil, and gas.
